extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and literary scholars interested in magical realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for identifying or producing works of magical realism: features of tone, setting, narrative stance, thematic uses (political/cultural), and how it differs from related genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition: realistic view with magical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Presents a realistic view of the world while incorporating magical or supernatural phenomena; magical elements are interwoven with mundane settings and treated as part of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genre 'presents a realistic view of the world while also incorporating magical elements, often blurring the lines between speculation and reality.' Often associated with novels (e.g., Gabriel García Márquez). The aim is typically to use the miraculous to make a point about reality rather than to create escapist fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial realistic detail / literary realism grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses a substantial amount of realistic detail and mimetic techniques so that the fantastic stands out against an otherwise convincing, everyday world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magical realism relies on realistic description and everyday detail so that supernatural events appear plausible in context. This grounding distinguishes it from much fantasy and helps the magical elements comment on real social/historical conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world setting (no invented worlds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are set in the existing, recognizable world rather than in fully invented secondary worlds; the supernatural invades or is revealed within ordinary settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers 'do not invent new worlds, but rather, they reveal the magical in the existing world.' For characters, extraordinary events are often ordinary and unremarkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial reticence / matter-of-fact presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator withholds explanations about the magical events, presenting them indifferently and with logical precision so the reader accepts the marvelous as normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined as 'the deliberate withholding of information and explanations about the disconcerting fictitious world.' The narrator's indifferent tone and lack of explanatory commentary prompt the reader to accept the fantastic as part of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastical realism elements (types of magic used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes specific magical phenomena—levitation, telepathy, telekinesis, ghosts, angels, mythic events—often drawn from folklore, fable, or myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements (e.g., telepathy, levitation) are integrated into the narrative to 'encompass modern political realities' or to bring fables/folk tales into contemporary relevance. Use of concrete fantastical traits helps link the magical to social meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' acceptance of the marvelous
rubrics_metrics.description: For characters within the story, magical or uncanny events are treated as ordinary facts of life rather than inexplicable miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key diagnostic: the implied characters do not react as if the supernatural is surprising; its ordinariness is central to the mode and distinguishes it from genres where magic triggers explicit wonder or crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenitude / baroque abundance of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency toward dense, layered, 'baroque' detail—an abundance of associative, disorienting material rather than empty, minimalist composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alejo Carpentier's notion of the baroque/plenitude: 'a lack of emptiness' and an 'extraordinary' abundance of detail that helps create the 'marvelous real'—useful for translating complex cultural/historical textures into fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridity / multiple planes of reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Plotlines frequently employ hybrid, overlapping planes of reality—mixing the rural and urban, Western and indigenous perspectives, and multiple cultural logics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magical-realist narratives often juxtapose inharmonious arenas and knowledge systems; hybridity becomes a structural tool to represent transcultural or postcolonial conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metafiction and textualization (reader/self-reflexiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses metafictional devices: stories within stories, fictional readers within the text, and moments where the textual world intrudes upon the real reader's world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textualization has two senses: a fictitious reader enters the story while reading it, and the textual world can enter the reader's world. This self-reflexiveness often supports political or social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened awareness of mystery / withholding exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative techniques encourage a state of heightened perception in the reader by omitting conventional exposition, linear causality, or scientific rationale for events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are asked to 'let go' of normal expectations and strive for 'a heightened awareness of life's connectedness' or the 'mystery that breathes behind things' (estado límite). The text may obfuscate or omit explanation to foster mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political critique and counter‑hegemonic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Magical realism often carries implicit criticism of social elites and dominant discourses; it functions as a subversive mode that represents marginalized perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'alternative world' created in magical realism can correct established viewpoints and articulate cultural resistance. Authors commonly use the mode to comment on colonialism, inequality, and historical injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of history and myth to rework collective experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Blends history and fantasy to reinterpret national or collective events, using the marvelous to render political or historical convulsions legible in new ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include works that link mythic elements to moments of national significance (e.g., Midnight's Children connecting telepathy to India's independence). Such blending helps express realities that ordinary realism might fail to capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology: metaphysical, ontological, anthropological
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed classification distinguishing: European 'metaphysical' (estrangement/uncanny); 'ontological' (matter‑of‑fact relation to inexplicable events); and 'anthropological' (native worldview vs Western rationality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Spindler's typology can be used diagnostically but is not absolute; texts may combine types and critics debate the cultural implications of each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lo real maravilloso (marvelous realism) distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Carpentier's 'marvelous real' treats the marvelous as endemic to a unidimensional world, whereas magical realism is bidimensional—supernatural blends with the familiar world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'marvelous' implies a world in which anything can happen (unidimensional); magical realism keeps two layers (bidimensional) so the miraculous coexists with the ordinary and is presented matter-of-factly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from surrealism
rubrics_metrics.description: Magical realism focuses on the material reality of the world and presents magic as part of it, whereas surrealism privileges the imagination, subconscious, dreams and psychological experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrealism seeks to express inner life and unconscious material; magical realism rarely frames the extraordinary as dreamlike or purely psychological, relying instead on tangible, material presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from fabulism
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabulism explicitly borrows from fables, myths and parables and tends to teach or allegorize; it often uses well‑known story elements, whereas magical realism more often uses general miraculous elements grounded in cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabulism is not tied to a single culture and often aims at moral exempla; magical realism is more likely to be politically inflected and grounded in specific historical/cultural experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: In fantasy the supernatural is often problematized and requires integration into a non‑realistic framework; in magical realism the supernatural is accepted and integrated into the ordinary without foregrounding explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amaryll Beatrice Chanady notes differences based on antinomy, integration into a logical framework, and authorial reticence. Magical realism accepts the supernatural as matter-of-fact, while fantasy often frames it as extraordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial/characterial 'attitude' as diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics define magical realism less by events than by an attitude — a stance toward the world expressed by characters or the narrative voice (e.g., Leal: 'an attitude on the part of the characters toward the world').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters treat the mysterious as part of existence and the narrative voice endorses that stance, the work leans towards magical realism; this emphasizes affective and perceptual orientation over checklist features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative voice and tone: objective narration and 'brick face'
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective, often deadpan or neutral narration ('brick face') that reports marvels without emotive or sensationalist coloring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: García Márquez advised writing the marvelous with the same neutral expression as storytellers who recount the supernatural as ordinary; this tone helps the reader accept the uncanny as normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to postmodern features
rubrics_metrics.description: Shares features with postmodernism—self‑reflexiveness, metafiction, intertextuality, multiplicity and destabilization of reader expectations—while remaining distinct in aims and cultural grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of these devices may align a text with both postmodern and magical-realist traditions; authors must balance intellectual subtlety with narrative accessibility.
